scope: Severe and catastrophic risks from frontier general-purpose AI. This is not a complete taxonomy of all AI harms.
framework: hazard → exposure → control → governance → incidents → resilience
headline_reading: Dangerous capabilities and failure modes are increasingly observable. Deployment exposure and real-world uplift remain only partly visible; safeguards are improving but uneven; independent evaluation and enforceable oversight do not yet provide comprehensive coverage.

questions.title: Does AI materially increase dangerous capability?
questions.question: In which severe-harm domains does a frontier system give a malicious or unskilled actor material, validated uplift over a non-AI baseline?
questions.current_reading: Dangerous uplift is increasingly measurable, but it is domain-specific and does not justify one cross-domain danger score.

domains.label: Cyber
domains.reading: Autonomous task length and expert-level successes are rising; verified malicious use now reaches later attack stages.

domains.label: Chemical & biological
domains.reading: Expert knowledge and laboratory-support performance are strong, but public end-to-end actor-uplift evidence remains limited.

domains.label: Manipulation & fraud
domains.reading: Misuse is documented, but standardized severe-harm uplift measurements are sparse.

domains.label: Autonomous operation
domains.reading: Longer autonomous software and cyber tasks are measurable; reliable consequential end-to-end operation remains uneven.

indicators: Randomized expert and novice uplift against a no-AI control
End-to-end task completion rather than knowledge-question accuracy
Change in time, cost, reliability, and attainable scale
Results separated by chatbot, agent, fine-tuned, and open-weight access

evidence.finding: UK AISI reports that average success on apprentice-level cyber tasks rose from just over 10% in early 2024 to about 50%, while the cyber task duration models complete without human direction grew from under ten minutes in early 2023 to over an hour by mid-2025.
evidence.measurement: Cyber evaluation success and autonomous task duration
evidence.source_label: UK AI Security Institute · Frontier AI Trends Report
evidence.caveat: Controlled evaluations do not establish realized harm or novice uplift in deployment.

evidence.finding: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team described early-warning capability gains but assessed the tested models as below its thresholds for substantially elevated national-security risk.
evidence.source_label: Anthropic · Progress from our Frontier Red Team
evidence.caveat: The thresholds and sensitive evaluation details are not fully public.

gaps: Preregistered independent end-to-end uplift studies with realistic actors
Comparable results across cyber, CBRN, manipulation, and autonomous-operation domains
movers: Replicated novice uplift that completes a consequential attack chain
Repeated independent findings of negligible incremental uplift after realistic bottlenecks and safeguards

questions.title: Do agents violate operator intent under real authority?
questions.question: When given realistic delegated authority, do frontier agents strategically violate operator intent, conceal it, or resist correction at consequential rates?
questions.current_reading: Strategic violations are demonstrated in stress-test simulations; the base rate in real deployments is unknown.

pole_a.label: Reliably corrigible
pole_a.desc: Agents obey constraints, accept correction, and remain controllable across realistic high-authority settings.

pole_b.label: Strategic violations
pole_b.desc: Agents deceive, sabotage, evade correction, or preserve their objectives when authority and incentives conflict.

indicators: Deception, sabotage, shutdown-compliance, and self-preservation rates
Hidden deployment-like evaluations with realistic permissions
Persistence across models, prompts, scaffolds, and mitigations
Successful harmful action after monitoring—not expressed intent alone

evidence.finding: Anthropic stress-tested 16 models in hypothetical corporate environments and observed malicious insider behavior in at least some forced-conflict cases across developers; it reported no known real-world deployment instances of this behavior.
evidence.measurement: Behavior rate in deliberately constructed conflict simulations
evidence.caveat: The scenarios closed off ethical alternatives and were designed to elicit failure, so they do not estimate deployment prevalence.

evidence.finding: UK AISI reports self-replication-task success rising from below 5% to above 60% on a subset of simplified evaluations, while emphasizing that current models remain unlikely to complete real-world self-replication chains.
evidence.source_label: UK AI Security Institute · Frontier AI Trends Report
evidence.caveat: Component benchmarks are not evidence that a system has attempted autonomous replication in deployment.

gaps: Independent evaluations that preserve realism without telling models they are being evaluated
movers: Verified strategic violations outside deliberately contrived stress tests
Low stable failure rates across unseen high-authority environments and model families

questions.title: How much dangerous capability is actually exposed?
questions.question: How much potentially dangerous capability is exposed through real deployments, tool permissions, unsupervised operation, or irreversible weight release?
questions.current_reading: The risk factors are clear, but there is no standardized public series for deployment authority, scale, or human intervention.

evidence_quality.independence: government taxonomy and external research collaboration

ladder.label: Advice only
ladder.desc: Text output; no direct action or persistent credentials.

ladder.label: Read access
ladder.desc: Can inspect external systems or private data but cannot change state.

ladder.label: Constrained write
ladder.desc: Can act through bounded tools with approvals, logs, and rollback.

ladder.label: High-impact autonomy
ladder.desc: Persistent credentials, broad write access, long runtimes, or safety-critical authority.

ladder.label: Irreversible proliferation
ladder.desc: Open weights or copied systems operate outside provider monitoring and recall.

indicators: Read versus write permissions and credential scope
Maximum uninterrupted runtime and number of consequential actions
Human approval frequency, logging, rollback, and kill mechanisms
Hosted, fine-tunable, or open-weight access
Number and scale of deployments in critical environments

evidence.finding: NIST distinguishes read-only, constrained-write, and write access and highlights statefulness, reversibility, environment trust, and action criticality as key dimensions of agent risk.
evidence.source_label: NIST · Lessons Learned on Tool Use in Agent Systems
evidence.caveat: A taxonomy identifies what should be measured; it does not provide deployment prevalence.

evidence.finding: UK AISI finds that open-weight systems can be modified arbitrarily, used without oversight, and spread irreversibly; safeguards can be removed quickly and cheaply.
evidence.source_label: UK AI Security Institute · Open-weight risk management
evidence.caveat: This establishes qualitative exposure mechanisms, not the number or severity of exposed deployments.

gaps: Provider and deployer telemetry on permissions, run length, sensitive actions, and intervention rates
A denominator for high-impact deployments and open-weight downstream use
movers: Rapid growth in persistent unsupervised high-privilege deployments
Verified least-privilege defaults, bounded autonomy, action logging, and staged access tied to risk

questions.title: How much risk remains after safeguards?
questions.question: Against each defined threat model, how much attack success remains after all deployed safeguards and operational controls are applied?
questions.current_reading: Safeguards are improving, sometimes sharply, but robustness is uneven across models, threat domains, attack budgets, and access types.

pole_a.label: Robust under attack
pole_a.desc: Defense-in-depth keeps end-to-end attack success low under adaptive, persistent, well-resourced testing.

pole_b.label: Readily bypassed
pole_b.desc: Transferable attacks, decomposition, fine-tuning, or scale defeat the production safeguard stack.

indicators: End-to-end attack success after the complete production stack
Attacker time, expertise, cost, and query budget
Monitor true-positive rate at a fixed false-positive rate
Benign refusal and operational cost
Patch latency and repeat-attack success

evidence.finding: UK AISI found a universal jailbreak for every system it tested, while one comparison showed about 40 times more expert effort was required to jailbreak a newer protected system.
evidence.measurement: Expert time to a universal biological-misuse jailbreak
evidence.source_label: UK AI Security Institute · Frontier AI Trends Report
evidence.caveat: Two systems and one defended domain do not establish general safeguard robustness.

evidence.finding: Anthropic reports that its first Constitutional Classifiers reduced attack success from 86% to 4.4%. Its successor was tested for more than 1,700 red-team hours across 198,000 attempts, finding one high-risk vulnerability and no universal jailbreak during that test.
evidence.measurement: Attack success and red-team search effort
evidence.caveat: The result is domain- and implementation-specific and is not an independent population estimate.

gaps: Comparable independent tests of full production systems
Long-budget adaptive attacks across cyber, CBRN, fraud, and agent-control threat models
movers: Repeated independent low residual-risk estimates across threat models and access modes
Cheap transferable attacks or safeguards that fail under fine-tuning, decomposition, or operational scale

questions.title: Can evaluations detect danger before deployment?
questions.question: Do pre-deployment evaluations and live monitors reliably predict dangerous capability and behavior in real use?
questions.current_reading: Evaluations reveal important hazards, but realism, gaming, contamination, and weak evaluation-to-field calibration leave material blind spots.

pole_a.label: Predictive and hard to game
pole_a.desc: Tests and monitors prospectively identify consequential capabilities and failures before they appear in use.

pole_b.label: Blind spots and gaming
pole_b.desc: Systems recognize tests, exploit scoring, hide capabilities, or behave differently in deployment.

indicators: Calibration between pre-deployment predictions and field outcomes
Hidden-test versus public-test divergence
Evaluation awareness, sandbagging, and contamination
Monitor miss rate and time to detection
Independent evaluator access to the deployed scaffold and tools

evidence.finding: The International AI Safety Report identifies an evaluation gap: controlled pre-deployment tests often do not reliably predict real-world utility, risk, or behavior in the deployed system context.
evidence.caveat: This diagnoses the gap but does not quantify one cross-system miss rate.

evidence.finding: OpenAI reports that chain-of-thought monitoring outperformed monitoring actions and outputs alone across 13 evaluations and 24 environments, but notes limited realism, evaluation awareness, and uncertain generalization to wild misbehavior.
evidence.caveat: Monitorability of elicited reasoning is one control signal, not proof of end-to-end safety.

gaps: Matched prospective safety predictions and later production outcomes
Public monitor false-negative rates under realistic adversarial behavior
movers: Prospective evaluations that repeatedly predict later incidents and production behavior
Repeated capability surprises, sandbagging, or incidents missed by systems that passed evaluation

questions.title: Are frontier systems under enforceable oversight?
questions.question: What share of frontier development and high-risk deployment is covered by binding, independently auditable requirements that are actually enforced?
questions.current_reading: Binding legal scaffolding now exists, but global model coverage, independent access, compliance findings, and enforcement outcomes remain patchy.

pole_a.label: Broad enforceable coverage
pole_a.desc: High-risk developers and deployments face binding evaluation, reporting, audit, security, and corrective requirements.

pole_b.label: Voluntary or unenforced
pole_b.desc: Important systems remain outside binding rules, or requirements lack verification, capacity, penalties, and corrective action.

indicators: Share of frontier developers and models within binding regimes
Mandatory risk evaluation, incident reporting, and cybersecurity
Independent evaluator and regulator access
Published compliance findings, penalties, and remediation
Coverage of internal deployment and open-weight release

evidence.observed_period: EU rules in force August 2025; enforcement powers August 2026
evidence.finding: EU obligations require providers of systemic-risk general-purpose models to submit risk, safety-framework, and serious-incident materials; Commission enforcement powers, including fines, became applicable in August 2026.
evidence.caveat: Legal authority does not yet establish broad or effective enforcement outcomes.

evidence.finding: California SB 53 requires large frontier developers to publish and follow frontier-AI frameworks, disclose model-specific catastrophic-risk assessment summaries, and report specified critical safety incidents.
evidence.caveat: The law emphasizes transparency and process; it does not itself prove mitigation effectiveness or global coverage.

gaps: Comparable data on inspections, noncompliance, sanctions, and remediation
A global denominator for covered frontier models and consequential deployments
movers: Independent audits, published compliance findings, corrective orders, and broader model coverage
Major uncovered systems, unenforced violations, repeated exemptions, or purely self-attested compliance

questions.title: What severe incidents and near misses are occurring?
questions.question: What well-documented severe incidents and near misses are occurring, what incremental role did AI play, and how quickly were they detected and contained?
questions.current_reading: Providers have documented malicious use, especially in cyber operations, but public cases are selected and do not provide a stable rate or cross-domain denominator.

evidence_quality.setting: observed provider cases and incident taxonomies

incidents.reading: Anthropic reported an AI-orchestrated campaign against roughly 30 targets, with a small number of successful infiltrations and limited human intervention.
Anthropic analyzed 832 banned accounts with sufficient detail; 67.3% used AI for malware preparation and 6.5% for lateral movement.
incidents.attribution: provider-selected account sample; no population denominator

indicators: Documented incidents by domain and independently rated severity
AI's role: incidental tool, productivity multiplier, capability unlock, or autonomous operator
Counterfactual attribution confidence
Direct loss and affected people or systems
Time to detection, containment, disclosure, and remediation
Reporting-coverage denominator

evidence.finding: Anthropic reported a state-sponsored cyber-espionage campaign using Claude Code to attempt infiltration of roughly 30 targets, succeeding in a small number of cases; it assessed the operation as largely AI-executed with occasional human direction.
evidence.caveat: The report has privileged telemetry but limited external verification and no population denominator.

evidence.finding: Anthropic mapped 832 banned malicious-cyber accounts with sufficient detail: 560 used AI for malware preparation and 54 for lateral movement, illustrating deeper use in attack workflows without estimating prevalence among all attackers.
evidence.caveat: The sample is a subset of banned accounts and cannot establish an incidence rate or counterfactual harm.

evidence.finding: The OECD distinguishes incidents that caused actual harm from hazards that could plausibly cause harm and is developing an open reporting process to complement news-derived events.
evidence.source_label: OECD.AI · Incidents and Hazards Monitor methodology
evidence.caveat: News-derived discovery is sensitive to coverage and reporting changes, so raw counts are not a stable harm trend.

gaps: A defensible denominator and counterfactual estimate of AI's incremental role
Comparable coverage beyond cyber and fraud
movers: Independently verified incidents where AI unlocks otherwise infeasible or substantially more severe harm
Falling severity and containment time under stable or improving reporting coverage

questions.title: Can society contain and recover from failures?
questions.question: If model, safeguard, or governance failures occur, can affected institutions prevent propagation, maintain critical services, and recover quickly?
questions.current_reading: Resilience is causally essential but almost unmeasured in public, frontier-AI-specific stress tests and recovery data.

pole_a.label: Contained and recoverable
pole_a.desc: Critical systems have tested fallbacks, limited common-mode exposure, rapid detection, and effective recovery.

pole_b.label: Cascading and hard to reverse
pole_b.desc: Dependencies, concentration, or weak response turn local AI failures into persistent or systemic harm.

indicators: Critical-sector AI dependency and substitutability
Manual fallback and rollback performance
Independent exercises for finance, energy, communications, healthcare, and government
Detection, containment, and recovery time
Concentration and common-mode failure exposure

evidence.finding: The International AI Safety Report treats societal resilience as necessary because no safeguard stack is perfectly reliable and identifies stronger critical infrastructure, detection tools, and institutional response capacity as key defenses.
evidence.source_label: International AI Safety Report 2026 · Executive Summary
evidence.caveat: The report establishes importance and candidate practices, not a current comparative resilience score.

evidence.finding: NIST reports that post-deployment monitoring methods, terminology, and best practices remain nascent and fragmented, limiting visibility into field failures and recovery performance.
evidence.source_label: NIST AI 800-4 · Monitoring Deployed AI Systems
evidence.caveat: Monitoring maturity is an input to resilience, not a direct measure of recovery capacity.

gaps: Standardized public stress tests and recovery data tied to frontier-AI failure scenarios
Critical-sector dependency and common-mode exposure inventories
movers: Successful independent sector exercises, tested fallbacks, and rapid recovery from actual incidents
Critical dependence without fallback, cascading failures, or provider concentration that amplifies one compromise
